description: We are a team of students from UNICEPLAC, Brasília, Brazil, passionate about technology, innovation, and learning. Our interests include software development, Python, React, AI, and data visualization. We aim to create innovative solutions using NASA's open data while gaining experience and growing together. We welcome curious, motivated teammates, especially those skilled in UI/UX, data science, and scientific research. Let's learn, collaborate, and build something meaningful!
summary:
SONATLAS — Explore Earth Through Sound is an interactive web platform that transforms NASA Earth observation data into meaningful visual and auditory experiences.

Developed for the "Earth Information Jukebox" challenge, SONATLAS explores data sonification as a way to make complex environmental information more engaging, understandable, and accessible.

Our initial focus is precipitation. Using real data from NASA's Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission and the IMERG dataset, we processed scientific observations from two tropical regions: the Central Amazon in Brazil and the Kisangani area of the Congo Basin in Africa.

Users can explore an interactive 2D map or 3D globe, visualize precipitation patterns over time, and hear scientific measurements translated into sound. Rainfall intensity controls sound frequency, while the proportion of rainy areas influences rhythmic pulses.

SONATLAS also incorporates accessibility features, including voice narration, keyboard navigation, and textual descriptions.

Beyond rainfall, our modular architecture offers opportunities to explore temperature, vegetation, air quality, and other environmental variables.

Our mission is simple: make Earth's scientific data not only visible, but also audible.
details:
SONATLAS — Project Details

1. Project Overview

SONATLAS — Explore Earth Through Sound is an interactive web application designed to transform scientific Earth observation data into visual, auditory, and accessible experiences.

Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, under the Earth Information Jukebox challenge, our project explores data sonification as an alternative way to communicate environmental information.

Our central question was:

What if we could not only see Earth's environmental changes, but also hear them?

SONATLAS combines satellite observations, geographic visualization, temporal exploration, and mathematical sound synthesis to help users discover patterns in environmental data.

Rather than replacing traditional maps and graphs, our platform complements them with an additional sensory dimension.

2. How Does SONATLAS Work?

The application follows a scientific data processing and visualization workflow.

Step 1 — Scientific Data Acquisition

We use precipitation observations from NASA's Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission, specifically the IMERG Early Run V07B product, accessed through NASA Earthdata and GES DISC.

For our prototype, we selected two tropical study areas:

  • Central Amazon, Brazil: A geographic sample near Manaus.
  • Congo Basin, Democratic Republic of the Congo: A geographic sample near Kisangani.

These locations demonstrate how the same scientific and technological architecture can be applied to different parts of the planet.

Step 2 — Scientific Processing

We processed 12 official HDF5 satellite data files using Python.

The processing pipeline extracts precipitation measurements, validates scientific metadata, handles missing values, and organizes the results into structured JSON datasets.

The system currently includes 18 spatial precipitation matrices, each containing 750 geographic grid cells, representing historical observations from January 1, 2024, at 30-minute intervals.

The application preserves the original scientific measurements and their temporal references.

Step 3 — Interactive Geographic Exploration

Users can navigate through an interactive 2D map powered by Leaflet or explore Earth using a 3D globe.

They can select a study region, inspect precipitation intensity, and move through available timestamps using an interactive timeline.

The precipitation layer displays geographic variations based on actual satellite-derived measurements rather than simulated weather patterns.

Scientific indicators and charts are synchronized with the selected period.

Step 4 — Scientific Sonification

Our sound engine uses the Web Audio API to convert environmental measurements into auditory parameters.

We defined transparent, deterministic relationships between the data and the generated sounds:

  • Precipitation intensity: Influences sound frequency. Higher precipitation rates produce higher-pitched tones.
  • Rainfall coverage: Influences rhythmic pulse density. Greater spatial coverage produces more pulses.
  • Missing data: Receives a distinct auditory indication to avoid confusing unavailable measurements with zero precipitation.

This approach allows users to listen to environmental variations while retaining access to their original numerical values.

3. Accessibility and User Experience

Accessibility was an important consideration throughout development.

SONATLAS incorporates:

  • Voice narration of scientific information.
  • Keyboard navigation.
  • Textual descriptions of observations.
  • Accessible representations of spatial data.
  • User-configurable accessibility preferences.
  • An educational audio guide explaining the platform.

Our goal is to provide complementary ways of exploring scientific information, including for users who encounter barriers with exclusively visual representations.

We recognize that further testing with assistive technologies and diverse users is necessary to evaluate accessibility comprehensively.

4. Technologies and Tools

SONATLAS was developed using a modular software architecture.

Frontend and Visualization

  • React and TypeScript
  • Vite
  • HTML5 and CSS3
  • Leaflet and GeoJSON
  • React Globe GL and Three.js
  • Interactive charts and temporal visualization

Scientific Processing and Geospatial Services

  • Python
  • NumPy and h5py
  • FastAPI
  • Shapely
  • NASA Earthdata and GES DISC
  • HDF5 and JSON data formats

Audio and Accessibility

  • Web Audio API
  • Web Speech API
  • Browser-based sound synthesis
  • Accessible interface components

Development and Quality Assurance

  • Git and GitHub
  • Vitest and pytest
  • Automated validation and integration testing
  • AI-assisted development tools under human supervision

The application runs in modern web browsers and does not require specialized hardware.

5. What Makes SONATLAS Creative?

SONATLAS brings together several approaches that are often explored separately: scientific data processing, interactive cartography, audio synthesis, and accessibility.

Its creativity lies in transforming numerical environmental measurements into an experience users can both see and hear.

Unlike an application that simply plays recordings of rain, SONATLAS generates sounds based on mathematical relationships with the underlying scientific data.

Another important aspect is geographic flexibility. The same architecture supports two study regions on different continents while maintaining consistent visualization and sonification rules.

The system also combines spatial and temporal perspectives: users can observe where rainfall occurs, follow changes over time, and listen to the corresponding measurements.

6. Benefits and Intended Impact

We envision SONATLAS contributing to three main areas.

Science Education

By combining sound, interactive maps, and scientific indicators, SONATLAS can help students and educators explore Earth observation data through hands-on learning.

Science Communication

The platform provides an engaging introduction to complex environmental datasets, encouraging curiosity about satellite observations and Earth science.

Accessibility and Inclusion

Sonification, voice narration, and textual alternatives can complement traditional visual representations and support more inclusive scientific experiences.

Our intention is not to replace conventional scientific analysis, but to expand the ways people can interact with environmental information.

7. Future Expansion

Precipitation is our first implemented environmental variable, but it is not the limit of the SONATLAS concept.

We selected rainfall because it is a familiar natural phenomenon with measurable spatial and temporal variations, making it especially suitable for demonstrating scientific sonification.

The modular architecture creates opportunities to integrate additional Earth observation datasets, including:

  • Temperature: Exploring thermal variations through sound.
  • Vegetation: Communicating changes in vegetation indices and ecosystem conditions.
  • Air quality: Representing variations in atmospheric indicators.
  • Other environmental phenomena: Exploring additional scientifically validated datasets.

Each new variable would require its own data validation procedures and carefully designed sound mappings.

Future developments may also include broader geographic coverage, additional observation periods, comparative analysis, and automated updates from scientific data sources.

8. Challenges and Scientific Considerations

Throughout development, our team prioritized scientific transparency and technical reliability.

We considered several important factors:

  • Using authentic, traceable NASA datasets.
  • Preserving geographic coordinates and observation timestamps.
  • Maintaining scientific measurement units.
  • Distinguishing missing observations from valid zero values.
  • Avoiding misleading interpretations of incomplete temporal series.
  • Ensuring that visual and auditory representations refer to the same scientific measurements.
  • Designing for accessibility and responsive devices.
  • Maintaining performance when rendering geographic data and interactive 3D elements.

Our current prototype uses historical observations rather than live weather monitoring or forecasting.

The selected geographic samples do not represent the entirety of the Amazon or Congo basins. We also recognize the uncertainty inherent in satellite-derived precipitation estimates and the importance of further independent scientific validation.

9. Conclusion

SONATLAS demonstrates how Earth observation data can become more approachable through the combination of scientific visualization and meaningful sound.

By transforming real NASA precipitation measurements into interactive geographic and auditory experiences, we aim to encourage curiosity, support education, and explore more inclusive approaches to science communication.

Our long-term vision is to develop SONATLAS into an expandable platform where different environmental phenomena can be explored through sound.
